news.title: Inside Jill Biden's fiercely guarded East Wing: Ugly blame game over 'catatonic' Joe... how the first lady would do anything to make the president 'look good'... and the 'work husband' who would 'crawl into a coffin with her'
news.text:
It was August 2021, and the disastrous fall of Kabul was underway, with the Taliban marching on the Afghan capital after President Joe Biden's chaotic withdrawal of US troops.

Everyone was mobilizing to try and help Afghans who had worked with the US military to escape, and former US first ladies were leaping into action. They had historically supported female empowerment in the country, aware that standing up for the rights of Afghan women was a cause that few could quibble with.

But even as rumors swirled that 'kills lists' of female Afghan activists were circulating, one emergency call at the White House allegedly had a different priority: how to shield First Lady Jill Biden from any political fallout.

'Hillary Clinton and Laura Bush mobilized their usual networks to mount independent missions to evacuate Afghan women,' author Azadeh Moaveni writes in a new book. 'But while Hillary and Laura were hard at work, Jill Biden appeared to have gone missing.'

The call is detailed in The East Wing: Power, Intrigue, and the Untold Story of America's First Ladies, in which Moaveni traces Jill's time in the position from its promising start to her alleged Lady Macbeth-esque role trying to keep her ailing husband in power when he was up for re-election.

Less than a year before the Kabul incident, the omens had been good when Jill's husband won the 2020 election, inheriting a country with a population that was bruised, exhausted and economically depressed after the Covid-19 pandemic and a tumultuous Trump presidency.

Schools and families were struggling to get back to normal, but 'Jill was one of the few messengers in the administration who resonated with mothers and teachers, who was a teacher herself,' Moaveni writes. She was also politically seasoned, having been at the side of her husband during his career as a senator then serving as Second Lady when he was Vice President to Barack Obama.

But there were early signs that her allegiances were not primarily to the American people, Moaveni claims, but to a husband she had married when she was 26 years old, and to a family which had gone through intense personal turmoil and tragedy. 

During Joe Biden's campaign for the presidency, Jill had visited the squalid Matamoros migrant encampment in Mexico just over the US border and penned an emotional op-ed in the Wall Street Journal asking, 'is this what we have become?' in Trump's America.

But within months of Biden assuming office, with migration on the southern border proving unpopular with voters, she quietly abandoned her initiative to reunite migrant families, a pattern she would repeat throughout her husband's presidency, The East Wing claims.

'Most First Ladies were like this to a degree. But Jill was singular in the way she subsumed herself into Joe's presidency,' writes Moaveni.

'She supported only causes that made him look good and abandoned them the moment they didn't. Any subject that proved awkward to the Biden administration she would generally avoid, even when it related directly to her brand as an educator and an advocate for women.'

Case in point, at the time of the aforementioned fall of Kabul, Jill was involved in an initiative called Joining Forces which supported military families, but in their hour of need, her team had other priorities, the book claims, which was to stop 'all activities that might expose the First Lady to public anger.'

'They had a huge fear of doing anything at bases, they were just petrified,' a former staffer told Moaveni. 'Even though this was when military communities needed support.'

Jill put out a statement mourning the loss of lives a day after a suicide bomb at Kabul airport killed 13 US Service members and more than 170 Afghan civilians, telling military families: 'My heart is with you as you navigate what comes next.'

She avoided any mention of the political ramifications of the withdrawal at the time, although she acknowledged in her recent biography, View From The East Wing, that the fall of Kabul was a 'turning point for Joe's administration.'

Jill's unerring loyalty can be traced back, Moaveni writes, to the start. When she married Joe in 1977, she inherited a family marked by tragedy. Biden's wife Neilia and their 13-month-old daughter Naomi were killed in a car accident five years earlier.

Their sons Hunter and Beau survived, and Jill had the difficult task of becoming 'both stepmother and substitute mother, tending to their lives as Joe commuted to Washington to build his political career.' 

In 1981, Jill and Joe's daughter, Ashley, was born, but personal upheaval and tragedy followed the three children into adulthood. Beau died of brain cancer in 2015. Both Hunter and Ashley struggled with addiction, with Hunter's very public meltdowns triggering a string of crises for the Bidens.

The book details how Joe and Jill initially refused to publicly acknowledge the existence of a little granddaughter called Navy Roberts, whom Hunter Biden had fathered between his marriages. It took a scathing New York Times article in 2023 for them to relent and speak about her.

The article by Maureen Dowd said the Bidens' reluctance to publicly embrace the child 'reveals is how dated and inauthentic the 80-year-old president's view of family is.'

A few weeks later, Joe Biden put out a statement saying he and Jill wanted the best for all their grandchildren, 'including Navy,' but it was 'not a political issue, it's a family matter.' Jill's recent biography is dedicated to her daughter and her granddaughters, but Navy is not listed among them.

The controversy highlighted how tangled their family life had become.

'Both Bidens were carrying out their roles while parenting adult children on the brink – of relapse into addiction, of legal and financial ruin,' writes Moaveni.

This desire to protect the family's privacy led to a number of political decisions, including the appointment of Anthony Bernal as Jill's senior advisor, a powerful gatekeeper variously described as Jill's 'work husband,' and the Biden 'marriage counsellor.'

His overriding attribute? Fierce loyalty to the Biden clan, and to Jill in particular.

'He never stopped wanting to hold her purse,' one insider told Moaveni. 'I think he would crawl into the coffin with her.'

The book goes on: 'Jill's approach to being First Lady was to act as Joe's lead messenger, and this suited Bernal. Her activities never took him out of his comfort zone. Instead, Bernal excelled as the guardian of the Bidens' privacy, and this made him indispensable and the sole staffer in the East Wing to hold real power.'

But by keeping a tight cabal of long-time loyalists and 'Biden people' around her rather than innovative thinkers, Jill was left with 'an aura of blandness,' the book observes: 'They were all respected hands but not the sort of brilliant policy minds, politicos and PR A-listers that Michelle Obama had brought in.' 

The result was an uninspiring tenure as First Lady in which projects including the migration initiative and funding for community colleges were championed then quietly dropped. 

Her initiative to provide free community college education failed when it was dropped from a broader spending bill, and while Jill said at the time that she was 'disappointed,' one insider told Moaveni: 'I didn't get the sense that she was on fire about it.'

'Over the course of four years, her First Ladyship unfolded as exceedingly narrow, even conservative,' Moaveni writes.

'She never pursued a distinct project through which the public could get a sense of her – of her personality, what she cared about and the texture of her beliefs and commitments. She stood steadfastly by her man and squeezed herself into such a narrow, Joe-centric persona that public opinion about the two of them essentially merged.'

But then came Joe Biden's declining health as he was running for a second term, and a chance for Jill to step in and prevent a looming electoral disaster for the Democratic Party.

In March 2024, some former White House staff started to raise the alarm, and the concerns mounted heading into the now infamous June 27, 2024, debate with Donald Trump.

The East Wing details how Jill was consumed in early June by Hunter's firearms trial and multiple official functions. At the same time, Joe developed a cold and appeared 'almost catatonic' to some big donors. He failed to recognize George Clooney, an incident about which the actor penned a scathing op-ed.

After Biden's stumbling and shambolic debate performance laid bare his age-related shortcomings, many questioned if Jill should have stepped in.

'Many senior Democrats blamed her, along with the rest of the family and his close aides, for hiding his condition,' Moaveni writes.

'Surely she had known how diminished he was, and if she knew, why had she not persuaded him to step down… as First Lady, she was the most intimate, public face of the campaign persuading Americans that he was fit to serve another term.'

Jill hailed her husband's debate performance and said he did 'such a great job.' But while she was publicly congratulating him, she admits in her recent biography that privately she was deeply concerned about her husband, and was worried he was having a stroke during the debate. 

She writes: 'It felt like we were watching an AI hologram of the man we knew, and the hologram was glitching.'

But at the time, even as the debate was attracting scathing feedback, she put on a brave face, appearing on the cover of Vogue four days later, wearing a Ralph Lauren tuxedo dress under the headline: 'We Will Decide Our Future.'

'The headline alluded to the rollback around women's rights, but landing four days after the debate, it appeared to convey that Jill was the key figure, along with Joe himself, in deciding the country's future,' the book observes.

While the magazine article had been planned months in advance, the decision to go ahead with it despite the awkward timing fueled the narrative of Jill as a 'Lady Macbeth' figure, so seduced by her proximity to power that she hid his age-related decline.

Even her political allies have dropped the reference, with Alexandra Pelosi, the daughter of former Democratic House speaker Nancy Pelosi, referring to her as Lady McBiden in 2025.

Jill has said during an appearance on The View last year that such comments were 'very hurtful' and said she did not have her husband 'sequestered in some place' to hide any cognitive decline.

The Daily Mail has reached out to Joe and Jill Biden for comment.

Joe Biden eventually stepped down as the Democratic candidate to make way for Kamala Harris at the end of July 2024, leading to Trump's resounding success at the election later that year and leaving Jill Biden with little legacy to speak of.

In her biography, Jill concedes that not adequately addressing concerns about Biden's health led to more questions, but she defends her time as First Lady and addresses the delicate tightrope she had to walk.

'Being First Lady could feel like a catch-22,' she writes. 'You were encouraged to use your platform to do good, but not to be too aggressive in pursuing policy goals, lest you be seen as overreaching. If you knew too little about what you were talking about, then you were an embarrassment. If you knew too much, you were trying to rule the world.
news.summary: There were early signs that her allegiances were not primarily to the American people, but to a husband and to a family which had gone through intense personal turmoil and tragedy.

news.title: Comment on Vance, Rubio, Ossoff and Buttigieg lead 2028 White House hopefuls by The Weekly Dispatch · Week to Sunday, 15 November 2026
news.text:
Four potential contenders in the 2028 race for the White House have caught American voters’ attention with their early jockeying: Republicans JD Vance and Marco Rubio and Democrats Jon Ossoff and Pete ​Buttigieg, according to the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll.

None of the four has yet formally launched a campaign and the parties’ 2028 nominating contests are more than a year away, leaving plenty of time ‌for new contenders to emerge and for voters’ views to change.

Some 45% of Republican voters polled said they believed Secretary of State Rubio would be an “excellent” presidential candidate, with 43% saying the same of Vice President Vance. Former Transportation Secretary Buttigieg and US Senator Ossoff, of Georgia, each got that rating from 29% of Democratic voters.

The poll, which surveyed 1,705 US adults nationwide including roughly 500 registered voters from each party and was completed on Monday, had a margin of error of 5 percentage points for Republican and Democratic ​voters.

President Donald Trump, struggling with an approval rating near the lowest of his career, looms large over the conversation for both parties. Republicans are divided on whether they want a candidate who breaks with Trump ​or follows in his footsteps, while Democrats, who are flying high after routing Republicans in the November 3 congressional elections, are divided on how aggressively to go after ⁠the president, such as through impeachment.

Trump has quizzed allies on whom they prefer Vance or Rubio and in a Sunday interview with CBS’s “60 Minutes” said he would “not necessarily” make an endorsement in the Republican primary.

‘MANAGED TO DO HIS ​JOB’

Barbara Rezner, an attorney in Florida who voted for Trump in the last three presidential elections, said she prefers Rubio over Vance, whom she considers too far to the right and too close to the president.

“Rubio has managed ​to do his job. He’s stayed off most people’s radar because he hasn’t done anything too far left, too far right, too crazy,” Rezner said.

The modest but growing dissatisfaction with Trump among Republicans is centered on the president’s decision to launch a war on Iran that has driven fuel prices higher. Rubio has been notably absent from many of the so-far fruitless peace talks with Iran despite being the nation’s top diplomat. Vance has shown signs of wanting to distance himself as well, saying publicly that the Republican drubbing ​in the midterm elections owed to the war with Iran.

A dozen-odd other Republicans are also in the national conversation over 2028 contenders, with Florida Governor Ron DeSantis among the best regarded, with 32% of Republicans rating him ​as an excellent option. Others – like Trump’s son, Donald Trump Jr., and Texas US Senator Ted Cruz – have their fans, but also many detractors.

Item 1 of 4 U.S. Vice President JD Vance President and Secretary of State Marco Rubio attend U.S. President Donald Trump’s address to the nation about election security, at the East Room of the White House in Washington, D.C., U.S., July 16, 2026. SAUL LOEB/Pool via REUTERS/File Photo

[1/4]U.S. Vice President JD Vance President and Secretary of State Marco Rubio attend U.S. President Donald Trump’s address to the nation about election security, at the East Room of the White House in Washington, D.C., U.S., July 16, 2026. SAUL LOEB/Pool via REUTERS/File Photo Purchase Licensing Rights, opens new tab

OSSOFF AND BUTTIGIEG

Among Democrats, Ossoff is at the top of many voters’ lists, with 29% of the party’s registered ‌voters rating ⁠him as excellent. Ossoff has grabbed headlines in recent months by calling Trump corrupt and unfit for office in unusually direct language, and last week he won his re-election race by 18 percentage points in Georgia, a state Trump carried by 2 points in 2024.

Buttigieg also gets the excellent rating from 29% of Democrats. Buttigieg also ran for president in 2020 and is better known nationally than Ossoff.

About one in five Democrats say they have never heard of Buttigieg, compared to roughly one in three who say the same about Ossoff. Very few Republicans are unfamiliar with Vance, but about one in six said they do not know who Rubio is. For candidates in either party, starting ​the election cycle with more name recognition can save ​money that would be spent getting the candidate’s ⁠name out, but examples abound of little-known candidates catching fire during the campaign, as happened with former President Bill Clinton.

Buttigieg and Ossoff are considered moderates among Democrats, and that appeals to Democratic voters like Ed Blair, a retired pig farmer in southern Illinois, who gives Buttigieg a better rating in part because Ossoff is less familiar.

“I do favor ​the more moderate candidates over the more progressive ones,” said Blair, who is wary of proposed major shifts like expanding federal Medicare health insurance coverage from ​all seniors to everyone in the ⁠country. Blair would prefer gradual shifts, such as expanding Medicare to cover all children. “In going towards some of the progressive policies, small steps need to be taken rather than large ones to give people time to adapt.”

The Reuters/Ipsos poll shows other well-known moderates – like former Vice President Kamala Harris, who lost to Trump in the 2024 presidential election, and California Governor Gavin Newsom – each get “excellent candidate” ratings of 23%, higher than the 15% of Democrats who view progressive stalwart Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, ⁠a US representative ​for New York, that way.

Ocasio-Cortez told CNN after the midterms that impeaching Trump should be an option on the table, while Buttigieg told the New ​Yorker magazine he is “not very interested” in impeachment.

Elaine Kamarck, a Democratic strategist, cautioned against reading too deeply into the public’s current views this far out from the 2028 election. “It’s a world away,” Kamarck said. “There are lots of people in both parties who are still deciding if they ​are going to run. You might be able to predict who will run, but you certainly don’t know anything about who is going to be ahead.”

Via Reuters

news.title: Analiza e CNN: Trump rrezikon t’i kushtojë sërish humbje republikanëve në vitin 2028
news.text:
Humbjet e thella të republikanëve në zgjedhjet e nëntorit 2026 kanë ngritur pikëpyetje të mëdha për të ardhmen politike të Partisë Republikane dhe ndikimin që presidenti Donald Trump mund të ketë në zgjedhjet presidenciale të vitit 2028.

Shtëpia e Bardhë dhe republikanët në Kongres duket se po nënvlerësojnë rrezikun që mund të sjellë popullariteti i ulët i Trump, edhe pse ai nuk do të jetë më në garë për një mandat tjetër presidencial.

Historia politike amerikane tregon se presidentët që largohen nga detyra me mbështetje të ulët publike shpesh rëndojnë ndjeshëm mbi kandidatin që synon t’i pasojë. Që nga fillimi i shekullit XX, sa herë që një president në largim është përballur me pakënaqësi të gjerë publike, partia e tij ka humbur zgjedhjet presidenciale pasuese.

Ky model është vërejtur në rastet e Woodrow Wilson në vitin 1920, Harry Truman në vitin 1952, Lyndon Johnson në vitin 1968 dhe George W. Bush në vitin 2008. Edhe Joe Biden, i cili u largua nga gara presidenciale e vitit 2024 mes pakënaqësisë së lartë publike, u pasua nga humbja e kandidates demokrate Kamala Harris përballë Trump.

Zgjedhjet e nëntorit 2026 duket se kanë dhënë një tjetër sinjal për këtë rrezik. Sipas të dhënave të sondazheve të votuesve të realizuara për CNN dhe media të tjera nga SSRS, 86% e votuesve që nuk miratonin performancën e Trump mbështetën demokratët në votimin kombëtar për Dhomën e Përfaqësuesve. Në garat kryesore për Senatin, kjo përqindje arriti në 85-89%.

Pakënaqësia ndaj presidentit ishte e përhapur në të gjithë vendin. Në 45 shtetet për të cilat disponoheshin të dhëna, shumica e votuesve mbështesnin performancën e Trump vetëm në pesë shtete me popullsi relativisht të vogël dhe prirje të fortë republikane: Arkansas, Idaho, Dakota e Jugut, Virxhinia Perëndimore dhe Uajoming.

Në shtetet ku demokratët fituan poste guvernatorësh apo vende në Senat, kundërshtimi ndaj Trump luajti një rol të rëndësishëm në formimin e koalicionit të tyre elektoral. Në Teksas, për shembull, 96% e votave të kandidatit demokrat për Senat, James Talarico, erdhën nga votues që nuk miratonin punën e presidentit.

Megjithatë, një humbje e madhe në zgjedhjet e mesmandatit nuk nënkupton automatikisht humbjen e zgjedhjeve presidenciale për partinë që kontrollon Shtëpinë e Bardhë. Në të kaluarën, disa presidentë kanë arritur të rikuperojnë mbështetjen pas rezultateve të dobëta, duke ndryshuar kursin politik ose duke përfituar nga përmirësimi i situatës ekonomike.

Harry Truman pas zgjedhjeve të vitit 1946 dhe Bill Clinton pas atyre të vitit 1994 janë dy shembuj të kësaj qasjeje. Edhe Ronald Reagan arriti të përfitonte nga rimëkëmbja ekonomike pas humbjeve republikane në vitin 1982.

Por situata aktuale e Trump paraqitet ndryshe. Ai vazhdon të përballet me pasojat politike të luftës me Iranin, ndërsa nuk ka dhënë sinjale për një ndryshim të rëndësishëm të kursit të tij. Përkundrazi, emërimi i Stephen Miller në postin e shefit të kabinetit të Shtëpisë së Bardhë dhe zgjedhja e Jim Jordan si drejtues i ri i republikanëve në Dhomën e Përfaqësuesve janë interpretuar si shenja të vazhdimit të së njëjtës linjë politike

news.title: Scott Colom’s Senate Win Is a Mississippi Miracle
news.text:
At the end of the night, though, Colom was up by twenty-eight votes. In the days that followed, as absentee and provisional ballots were processed, his lead crept past a thousand, then two, then four. On Wednesday, eight days after the election, Colom led by nearly five thousand votes, a wider margin than Hyde-Smith could overcome, and she conceded.
A victory rally was quickly arranged at Tougaloo College, in Jackson, the capital, where Colom and his campaign staff had been operating out of the former headquarters of the Mississippi Democratic Party. A berobed choir assembled. Supporters waved placards that read “SENATOR-ELECT SCOTT COLOM.” Bennie Thompson, who has long been Mississippi’s lone Black congressman, took the stage and noted how fitting it was to be celebrating at Tougaloo, a “safe haven for people who wanted to do right” and to “make this state a better place.” (Tougaloo was founded, in 1869, by Christian missionaries with the goal of educating freed slaves.) “All my friends kept saying, ‘I don’t know if the time is right. Maybe you’re moving too fast. Maybe he’s too young,’ ” Thompson told the crowd. “Well, well. Here we are, with a winner.” Thompson had been calling it “poetic justice” that Hyde-Smith—who once appeared in a Facebook photo wearing a Confederate hat, at the homeplace of Jefferson Davis, the President of the Confederacy, captioned “Mississippi history at its best!”—had helped engineer her own downfall. In 2023, she blocked Colom’s appointment, by then President Joe Biden, to the federal bench, thereby freeing him up to challenge her.
Only two Black senators had ever served Mississippi: Hiram Revels and Blanche Bruce. Both were sent to Washington, D.C., during Reconstruction, by the state legislature. This makes Colom the first Black senator ever elected by the people. “All I did was have the courage to imagine a night like this,” he said at the victory rally. “I had the courage to believe in Mississippi.”
Colom made his campaign slogan “Mississippi Matters” and used it to draw a contrast with Hyde-Smith. “Mississippi didn’t matter enough for her,” he told me. “She supported tariffs. She supported cutting health care. She voted against the bipartisan infrastructure bill. If you’re looking out for Mississippi, you wouldn’t do these things. Partisan politics were too important to her.” (Hyde-Smith called herself a “rock-solid conservative.”) Confidants tried to talk Colom out of the slogan, pushing alternatives such as “Mississippi Rising.” But he never wavered. “I felt like God had given it to me,” he explained. “God was proving me right, because when I started doing man-on-the-street videos, I realized it was something I could get anybody to say.”
To national party leaders and the media, Mississippi apparently didn’t matter, until it was almost too late. For the better part of two years, Colom waited for outsiders to take him seriously. As late as last week, he was still such an unknown that he was having to teach America how to pronounce his name: “kuh-loam,” not “coll-um.” The first time I met him, four days after the election, he said, “Where were you months ago?” He let me spend a minute with him not because of what’s on my business card but because I’m from Tupelo, in northeast Mississippi, which isn’t far from where he lives, in Columbus, with his wife, Nadia, a real-estate agent, and their daughters, Luci, who turns ten in December, and Madi, who is eight. Colom’s conversations always lead back to Mississippi. When he asked how I “got to The New Yorker,” and I joked that I’d “kicked the door down,” he noted, “That’s a value in Mississippi—persistence. We’re so disadvantaged, in so many ways, because ever since cotton stopped being a dominant commodity, we’ve never really had a strong economy.” What’s the answer to that? I asked. He replied, “Honestly, we gotta figure it out.”
Hyde-Smith had done little to no campaigning, and refused to participate in a debate. Colom’s staff made “THE WHERE’S CINDY TOUR” placards and, on social media, referred to her as “Cindy Hide-Smith.” Colom appeared in many dozens of town halls and campaign stops across Mississippi’s eighty-two counties. Nadia recalled him coming home “tattered with exhaustion.” Often, no one showed up to hear him speak. Colom told me about holding a press conference outside a hospital in Clarksdale, in the Delta, where he “tried to talk about the cuts to Medicaid, and how it impacts rural health care.” No reporters. “The local press is decimated,” he said.
Colom kept talking about “the math in Mississippi,” which has some of the most racially polarized voting in the country. Around thirty-seven per cent of the state’s population is Black; nearly all vote Democrat. Three-quarters of the white population votes Republican. Colom knew that he would need to persuade some of them. “You’re saying these people won’t vote for us—when they’re getting their health care cut, and they got tariffs hurting farmers, and costs through the roof?” he said. “You don’t try to get their vote, you’re basically telling them, I don’t care that this stuff is happening to you.”
By the end of the summer, polls showed Democrats up by double digits nationally. Colom was still projected to lose in deep-red Mississippi—but the margin was shockingly narrow. “The Democratic Party was not supporting him until they were, like, ‘Oh, wow, the polling data is real,’ ” Arekia Bennett-Scott, the executive director of Mississippi Votes, a nonpartisan civic-engagement organization in Jackson, told me. In late October, the Party finally sent cash—a modest two million dollars—and backup. Kamala Harris campaigned in Clarksdale and Columbus; Bill Clinton appeared in Tupelo. “Pete Buttigieg, I begged that guy to come,” Colom told me. “He’s, like, ‘You think it’s gonna help?’ I said, ‘Man, I know it’s gonna help, because if you come down I’m gonna do a press conference about how she didn’t vote for the bipartisan infrastructure bill but was at the Amtrak reopening, with Mardi Gras beads on, expecting people not to remember.’ ” He was talking about an appearance that Hyde-Smith had made, in August, 2025, for the relaunch of Amtrak’s Gulf Coast route, four years after opposing legislation that had provided nearly two hundred million dollars in funding for the project.
Buttigieg, who directed billions of dollars to Amtrak as Biden’s Transportation Secretary, is also a Navy veteran. This may have helped Colom with voters on the coast, which is home to major defense contractors such as Ingalls Shipbuilding, in Pascagoula. “Tell her about Ingalls shipyard,” Colom said to his political director, Theresa Kennedy, on Tuesday, as a sheriff’s deputy drove us, in a black S.U.V., to an event at a fire station on Medgar Evers Boulevard, in Jackson. Kennedy, sitting in the front seat, holding two flats of doughnuts that Colom planned to present to the firefighters, told me that her dad had worked at Ingalls for more than twenty years. She remembered him getting up for his shift at three or four in the morning. “Those people work really hard,” she said. During the campaign, Kennedy had arranged an appearance at Ingalls, and drove Colom through the night to get there as he slept in the passenger seat.
Colom’s family jumped in, too. Nadia appeared in campaign ads and operated a branded food truck, parking at music festivals and housing projects, and at factories, during shift changes, to hand out free meals. The signature dish was Pick Another Protein Tacos. The name derived from a moment, early this year, when Hyde-Smith replied to an interview question about the high price of beef by saying, “You know, you have so many proteins to choose from.” In February, Sarah Adlakha, a doctor and Chicago native who tried to unseat Hyde-Smith in the Republican primary, put out a campaign ad: between bites of hamburger, she says, “If I can’t afford beef, I should pick another protein? Or we could pick another senator.”
The Colom campaign repurposed the bit. Colom’s identical twin, Andrew, helped write a script for a new ad. They shot it in Columbus and featured locals, including a white guy, grilling beef patties, who says, “Pick another protein? Shiiiiiiit, I’d rather pick another senator instead,” and an older Black woman, eating at a restaurant, who says, “Pick another protein? She done lost her damn mind.” The ad—made in a few hours, for less than a thousand dollars—went viral.
Then he said, “Y’all wanna go live at five with me on CNN?” The correspondent Annie Grayer was there, ready to do a standup. Albert Fujii, Colom’s comms director, had expected the standup but not the group invite. He turned to me and said, “We go with the flow around here.” As the firefighters followed Colom to the front of a parked fire engine, one called out, “When you get to Washington, don’t forget about the common people!”
Waiting for Jake Tapper to cue Grayer into his broadcast, Colom told her, “I’m glad you’re getting to see Mississippi.” They chatted about troubling anecdotes that they’d heard, involving voters’ experiences at the polls, and Colom said, “We have to make it easier for people to vote.” Mississippi puts up more barriers to voting than almost any other state—there’s no online voter registration, no Election Day registration, no early voting. In March, Mississippi Today uncovered a new obstacle: the state has been vetting voter rolls using credit data from Experian, a consumer-reporting agency, which “guesses consumers’ possible addresses.” Experian’s own executives cautioned against using the data for election purposes, but the state carried on; some two hundred and thirty thousand voters, rendered “inactive,” vanished from precinct poll books, in part because of discrepancies in the data.
Those voters, on Election Day, could fill out a provisional ballot—called an affidavit ballot, in Mississippi—and track its progress on the secretary of state’s website. But scores of them learned that their ballot had been rejected, with little or no explanation. Colom told Grayer, “I hope the country’s starting to see why we can’t allow elected officials to use credit agencies to check the voter rolls.” Calling out Michael Watson, the secretary of state, he said, “This is the chaos that he created. He needs to be answering some tough questions.” (On X, Watson said that he stands by “our decision and the work we’ve done to clean up our voter rolls.”)
Colom had his patter down by now. When Grayer asked him how he’d been able to win over voters, he replied it helped that Trump had “betrayed” them, saying, “He promised lower prices on Day One, and the exact opposite happened. We had the highest increase in sales tax on Day One, through tariffs. He promised no more endless wars. We’re back at war.” (The resulting higher diesel prices were hurting farmers and truckers.) “He promised there would be a full release of the Epstein files. Well, he did everything except fully release the Epstein files,” he went on, adding, “We’re dealing with record levels of corruption.” The people of Mississippi “stood up for themselves and said, ‘We want to go in a new direction.’ ”
Back in the S.U.V., Colom told me, “To do what it takes, to actually win, everybody in politics has to have a little bit of a selfish motivation. I wanted Mississippi to get better representation, but my selfish motivation was I wanted to make my parents proud.” His parents, Dorothy and Wilbur, are both lawyers. His mother, a retired judge, was the first Black chancery-court judge elected in her four-county district, and has taught African American studies at Mississippi State, the alma mater of Gerard Henderson, Colom’s campaign manager.
Colom’s father goes by WOC, the initial letters of his full name, Wilbur O’Neal Colom. WOC, who is in his late seventies, is a former Republican and once worked on Ronald Reagan’s transition team. Colom introduced me to him at campaign headquarters, and we sat for a while, talking, as Colom, in the next room, appeared live on Chris Hayes’s show. When I asked WOC why he’d worked for Reagan, he grinned and said, “Thad Cochran talked me into it.” He was referring to the former longtime Republican senator from Mississippi, who, WOC recalled, had taken notice of his field-organizing skills. “I was always the most liberal guy in the Republican Party,” he told me, adding that “they never really seemed to care” about his politics, or his race. He used to tell his children, “Race is a first impression. They’ll have stereotypes about you when they first meet you, and then after they know something else, color falls to the side, because they’ve got too many other things to evaluate you on.”
I asked how else his children were raised. “Daddy gives no false praise,” he replied. “They used to say I was the toughest man on earth.” Scott is the older twin, by seconds. As a youth, he was “the peacemaker,” and played basketball. Andrew, who was “the most political,” served as student-body president. Andrew went to Columbia; Scott, before attending law school at the University of Wisconsin, went to Millsaps, a private college in Jackson. “He always wanted to be sort of close by,” WOC said.
Campaign staffers were lurking, probably to make sure we weren’t gabbing about anything sensitive. But we were talking only about the Colom homestead (“We’ve been in the same place since the family was freed as slaves”); and polio (rolling up his pants, he showed me that his left leg is smaller than his right leg, and said that he contracted the disease in 1952, three years before a vaccine became available); and Falkner, Mississippi (good basketball, back in the day); and Ripley, Mississippi, where my dad once went looking for our family’s golden retriever because people who stole dogs were known to sell them at a popular flea market there. WOC said, “They’re probably from Biggersville.”
I spent much of Monday and Tuesday in Madison County, which includes prosperous suburbs just north of Jackson. In 2024, Trump won Madison by seventeen points, but Colom had a slender lead. The county seat is Canton, which has a picturesque town square where movies get made. When I was there, film crews were setting up for “Don’t Open the Door,” a horror movie starring Omar Benson Miller, Ron Livingston, and Beverly D’Angelo. Five election commissioners, who are elected to four-year terms, were working next door to the shooting location, in a former Fred’s, a defunct regional discount chain and pharmacy. In their office suite—at the end of the one hall, past a Pepsi machine and shrink-wrapped towers of new license plates—someone had put up “QUIET ZONE” signs and cordons. A half-dozen election monitors were sitting or standing behind the cordons, silently recording the proceedings and making notes, as if studying creatures at a zoo.
The commissioners, sitting in pairs, were checking affidavit ballots against information on the screens of their Dell desktop computers, then running the ballots through tabletop scanners. The computers were arranged so that their audience could not see the screens, and the commissioners were speaking in voices too low for the monitors to hear. As I first walked in, just after eight in the morning on Monday, one monitor, Guy Gillespie, an attorney, was complaining to Spence Flatgard, a lawyer for Madison County who serves on Mississippi’s Judicial Election Oversight Committee, that the commissioners were violating state law. Flatgard told Gillespie, “We’re just going to have to agree to disagree.” When Gillespie told him to “pray about it for a minute,” another monitor turned to me and said, “That’s so Mississippi.”
An election monitor named Janine was spending long days observing the commissioners work. “They’re not that computer-savvy, and any kind of disruption rattles them,” she whispered to me. “I think the whole Experian thing is throwing them off.” One voter had just visited the office and learned that his vote would not count because he supposedly lived in California, she told me. “He said he’d never lived in California in his life.”
I eventually left, and when I came back Gillespie was stepping out, looking upset. “Something needs to be done,” he said. “The election laws in the state have got to be changed.” Deborah Ellis, a retired commercial insurance agent, had just come to ask why her affidavit had been rejected. When she started to explain her situation to the commissioners, one of them shushed her.
Ellis and I sat, chatting, on a bench in the corridor. She had on black pants, Hoka tennis shoes, and a patterned blue-and-white shirt, and she had gone to great trouble to be there—she was using a walker because she’s about to have spinal surgery. “I mean, I try to be involved, and do my own research,” she told me. But this matter had flummoxed her. She said that she had gone to vote, on Election Day, at St. Joseph Catholic Church, her voting precinct for at least twenty-one years, and was told that she needed to be at a different precinct. This was news to her—she had received no letter about it. After filling out an affidavit ballot, she had “left, thinking it was handled,” she told me. Yet the experience had left her so unsettled that she’d gone onto the secretary of state’s website, to make sure that her ballot was counted, and that was how she learned that it had been rejected.
When I asked whom Ellis had voted for, she gently declined to say. I was trying to find Republicans who had flipped for Colom; Janine, the election monitor, happened to pass by, and both women said good luck with that. Flippers were not likely to publicize their decision, especially in counties as historically red as Madison.
Each county manages its own election process, following state law. The vibe varies from place to place. In Hinds, a deep-blue county that includes Jackson, and which would eventually secure Colom’s win, election commissioners were setting out aluminum trays of fried catfish and chicken wings drenched in an eye-watering hot sauce. A commissioner named Kidada Brown, a retired high-school government teacher, was listening to DJ Curt, on TikTok, and explaining the affidavit process to anyone who wanted to learn. She wore a high, braided bun, a pink jumpsuit, a cropped denim jacket, geometric hoops, and glasses, and was using a pink felt-tip pen to write her conclusions across each affidavit ballot—“Not Found,” “Accepted,” “Rejected”—after checking the written information against the state’s data on her computer.
“Look at that—we found her! There she go. She voted in the correct place. That’s it, that’s her, we gonna accept her,” she said, finishing one case. For another, she picked up the phone, called the voter, and told him, “We trying to do your affidavit. You got purged off the voter roll ’cause you ain’t voted since 2018.” She let him know that casting an affidavit ballot had put him right, and chided him to “go on and vote,” in the future.
During the call, Brown discovered that the man’s address had been misspelled in the state’s database. She corrected it and reiterated, “Whatever you do, I want you to vote!”
Taylor, the N.A.A.C.P. director, told me, “I think we could’ve got here before now, but it required investment.” Throughout the entire Senate campaign, ad spending in support of Colom totalled some four to five million dollars. In Texas, another Democratic flip, spending for James Talarico neared a hundred and fifty million. “Scott Colom’s grit and grind won this race,” Taylor said. The win may loosen up more money for 2027, when Mississippi holds its next round of statewide elections. Taylor told me, “I wouldn’t mind getting a governor that I’m proud of.”
I first met Taylor in March of 2020, when I was covering a Biden campaign stop in Jackson; he invited me to Mississippi’s N.A.A.C.P. headquarters, at the Masonic Temple, on John R. Lynch Street, a landmark of the civil-rights movement. Walking me into the auditorium where the founders of the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party held their state convention, in the summer of 1964, he said, “Just being in a space where folks struggled with our ideas, and at a time when it was dangerous to voice them—it’s almost like you can feel their prayers when we’re doing our daily work.”
His late grandfather, a judge in Yazoo County, used to say that a politician starts campaigning the day he is born. “How you showed up before you decided to run will be foundational,” Taylor explained. In the Black community,“you get elected two ways.” One is long-term relationships. The other is what he calls the “trusted voice”—the one who says, “This is the person we think is best to represent our community. That’s the thing white liberals miss, especially those who are not from the South. They underestimate us, and assume we’re not organized in our community. Black communities have been organized since slavery.” Taylor’s grandfather also used to say, “You have to put your hands in the hands of the people.” This is what Colom did, up and down Mississippi.
Colom received several thousand more votes than Kamala Harris did in the state, in 2024, despite the fact that turnout typically drops substantially in midterm elections. Bennett-Scott, the Mississippi Votes organizer, told me that what “pushed it over the edge was Callais.” This spring, a landmark 6–3 U.S. Supreme Court decision, in Louisiana v. Callais, contributed to the ongoing erosion of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 by making it significantly easier for states to redraw district boundaries in a way that disadvantages voters of color. After the ruling, Tate Reeves, Mississippi’s Republican governor, announced his intention to end Thompson’s “reign of terror” in the Second District, an outcome that organizers are preparing to fight.
Suppressing the Black vote—and keeping people like Thompson, and now Colom, out of power—has historically been a significant part of Mississippi’s playbook. It is impossible to note this moment without remembering the Reverend George Lee, an N.A.A.C.P. branch co-founder who was assassinated after leading local voter-registration drives (Belzoni, Mississippi, 1955); Lamar Smith, a First World War veteran and voting-rights activist who was shot dead in broad daylight outside the Lincoln County Courthouse, after helping Black residents fill out absentee ballots (Brookhaven, Mississippi, 1955); Emmett Till, a fourteen-year-old Chicagoan who was tortured and killed after supposedly whistling at a white woman (Money, Mississippi, 1955); Herbert Lee, an N.A.A.C.P. charter member and voter-registration activist who was shot and killed by a state lawmaker and member of the violently racist White Citizens’ Council while delivering cotton to a gin (Liberty, Mississippi, 1961); Fannie Lou Hamer, a sharecropper and Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party co-founder who was beaten by law-enforcement officers after a voter-education workshop (Winona, Mississippi, 1963), and whose later declaration “We are sick and tired of being sick and tired” was a pivotal moment in the civil-rights movement; Medgar Evers, the state N.A.A.C.P. field secretary (whose office Charles Taylor inhabits today), who was shot dead in his driveway, by the racist fertilizer salesman Byron De La Beckwith (Jackson, Mississippi, 1963); James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner, Freedom Summer volunteers who were abducted and murdered by members of the Ku Klux Klan, including law-enforcement officers, while investigating the torching of a Black church (Philadelphia, Mississippi, 1964); Vernon Dahmer, the N.A.A.C.P. president in Forrest County, who died after Klansmen firebombed his home and grocery store, following his public offer to pay poll taxes for anyone unable to afford them (Hattiesburg, Mississippi, 1966). Forrest County, in southern Mississippi, is named for Nathan Bedford Forrest, who founded the Klan. Colom flipped it. ♦

news.title: Trump sank the GOP in 2026. He could do it again in 2028
news.text:
Judging by their choices since this month’s Democratic sweep, both the White House and congressional Republicans are vastly underestimating the party’s risk in 2028 if President Donald Trump remains as unpopular as he is now.

Dazed Republicans picking through the wreckage of their losses may console themselves with the thought that Trump’s dire approval ratings won’t pose as large a threat to the GOP in 2028, since he will be leaving the White House. But history strongly suggests that confidence is misplaced.

Outgoing presidents have cast a larger shadow than even many political professionals assume in the election to succeed them — especially when that retiring president faces widespread public discontent, as Trump does now. While popular outgoing presidents haven’t always ensured victory for their designated successors, the inverse has almost always been true: When the outgoing president is unpopular, his party has rarely won the election to replace him.

This month’s election underscored the danger looming for Republicans if Trump remains this weak. In House, Senate and gubernatorial elections across the country, the vast majority of voters who disapproved of Trump’s job performance — usually at least 80% of them — voted against Republican candidates, according to the most recently updated numbers as of November 12 from the Voter Polls conducted for CNN and other media organizations by SRSS.

“This massive repudiation of Republican candidates is totally and completely about Donald Trump,” said longtime GOP pollster Whit Ayres.

Even big losses in a midterm don’t guarantee defeat for the party holding the White House in the next presidential election. But presidents who have recovered from a bad midterm have usually changed direction in response to the rebuke (like Harry Truman after 1946 or Bill Clinton after 1994) or benefited from changing circumstances (as Ronald Reagan did when the economy recovered after his party’s poor 1982 midterm).

Trump, by contrast, remains caught in a grinding war against Iran with no clear exit. And far from adjusting his course, he has reaffirmed it with the appointment of Stephen Miller, his most ideologically extreme senior adviser, as White House chief of staff. House Republicans have responded to their losses in a similar way by choosing pugnacious Rep. Jim Jordan as their new leader.

“Donald Trump is going to double down and triple down” on the policies and style that alienated voters this year, said Steve Schmidt, a longtime GOP strategist who has become a staunch Trump critic. “Any person with any attachment to real life would look at this election and say, ‘Well, they certainly should have gotten the message and they’ll be chastened,’ but that doesn’t appreciate the physics of politics, which is that as an extreme party gets smaller, it becomes more fanatical.”

History is clear on the consequences

Novelist Leo Tolstoy famously wrote that every happy family is alike, while every unhappy family is different. The relationship of outgoing presidents to the election to succeed them inverts that maxim: The impact of every unsuccessful president has been largely the same, while the role of successful presidents has diverged.

Good feelings toward popular retiring presidents Theodore Roosevelt in 1908 and Ronald Reagan in 1988 helped each man’s designated successor win election. But despite very strong job approval ratings, both Dwight Eisenhower in 1960 and Bill Clinton in 2000 saw their vice-presidents lose nail biters (although Al Gore, Clinton’s No. 2, did win the popular vote). Barack Obama in 2016 wasn’t as popular as Eisenhower or Clinton, but he also left office with majority approval — only to see his party’s designated heir, Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, lose another tight race to Trump (despite, like Gore, winning the popular vote).

But when an outgoing president has lost the public’s support, the record is far more consistent. Since the turn of the 20th century, each time an outgoing president has been broadly unpopular, his party has lost the race to succeed him. That was true for Democrats Woodrow Wilson in 1920, Harry Truman in 1952, Lyndon Johnson in 1968 and Biden in 2024, as well as for Republican George W. Bush in 2008.

According to the exit polls conducted for CNN and other media organizations, 88% of the voters who disapproved of Reagan in 1988 and Clinton in 2000 voted for the other party’s presidential candidate. In 2016, 89% of voters who disapproved of Obama voted for Trump; in 2024, 82% of voters who disapproved of Biden voted for Trump over Vice President Kamala Harris.

Trump’s two victories help explain why a popular outgoing president is no guarantee of success for his party — while an unpopular retiring president has been a more reliable kiss of death.

In 2016, according to the exit polls, Obama’s approval remained at or just above 50% in each of six swing states he had won in 2012. But Trump still flipped all of them — Iowa, Ohio, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and Florida. The reason is that Trump captured a significantly larger share among the minority of voters who disapproved of Obama than Clinton won among the majority who approved. Trump harnessed virtually all the discontent about Obama, while Clinton’s own vulnerabilities prevented her from capturing as much of his support.

In 2024, the equation for Harris proved much more straightforward — and treacherous. Between 56% to 60% of voters in the seven major swing states disapproved of Biden’s performance and between 81% to 87% of those disapprovers backed Trump, powering him to victory in all of them, the exit polls found. Harris made missteps as a candidate, but her biggest problem was that pervasive discontent with the administration in which she served.

In recent times, the presidential nominee who had the most success separating from an unpopular outgoing president of his own party was Republican Sen. John McCain in 2008. Running against Obama, McCain won 30% of voters nationwide who disapproved of George W. Bush, the exit polls found.

As a senator who had occasionally clashed with Bush — and ran a bitter race against him for the GOP nomination in 2000 — McCain wasn’t intrinsically tied to his predecessor as closely as Harris, Gore and George H.W. Bush (who all served as vice presidents to the retiring president) or Hillary Clinton, who worked as Obama’s secretary of state. “There were famously enmities there,” between McCain and Bush, noted Schmidt, McCain’s chief strategist in the 2008 race.

Yet Schmidt said the campaign recognized it would take dramatic, even unprecedented, actions to overcome the public’s disapproval of Bush — which reached a stunning 71% in the 2008 exit poll amid fatigue with the Iraq War and fear and anger over that year’s financial crisis.

“It drove everything as a political consideration because you knew that there was a day of reckoning where you had to disrupt that headwind and fly out of it,” Schmidt said. That impulse, he said, drove McCain’s attempt to name Democrat-turned independent Sen. Joe Lieberman as his running mate. “It was going to take something like that to arrest the trajectory,” Schmidt recalled. (When Republicans rebelled over Lieberman, McCain abruptly pivoted to choosing Alaska Gov. Sarah Palin instead.)

In the end, even McCain could not paddle nearly fast enough to escape the undertow of Bush’s capsizing presidency. Obama that year won a higher share of the popular vote than any Democratic nominee since Johnson in 1964 and flipped nine states that had voted for Bush in 2004. In all of them, at least two-thirds of voters disapproved of Bush’s performance — and at least two-thirds of those disapprovers backed Obama.

The GOP’s 2028 conundrum

Through 2026, the one discordant sign for Democrats was polling consistently showing they were not winning nearly as many voters who disapproved of Trump as during his first term.

Democrats this year didn’t fully match the benchmarks they hit among Trump disapprovers in his first term. But ultimately Democrats carried about the same share of voters who disapproved of Trump as the opposition party did among voters who disapproved of Obama in 2010, Bush in 2006 and Bill Clinton in 1994. In the 2026 CNN Voter Poll measuring preferences in the national House popular vote, 86% of voters who disapproved of Trump backed Democrats; the party also won 85% to 89% of voters who disapproved of Trump in almost all the major Senate contests.

That was plenty to power a Democratic landslide. Disapproval of Trump in this election was not only deep (at 63%, his national disapproval rating was considerably higher than those other presidents in their worst midterm elections), but also broad. Across the 45 states where Voter Poll data is available, most voters approved of Trump’s job performance in only five sparsely populated deep-red states — Arkansas, Idaho, South Dakota, West Virginia, and Wyoming.

In every state where Democrats flipped a governorship, a Senate seat, or both, a substantial majority of voters disapproved of Trump’s job performance — and those disenchanted voters provided the core of the winning Democratic coalition. In Texas, for instance, 96% of the votes for Democratic Senate victor James Talarico came from people who disapproved of Trump.

One reason Republicans could not surmount the Trump discontent in 2028 was that so few displayed any independence from him. As Ayres noted, Republicans concluded that if they clashed with Trump, he would either hound them out of the party or defeat them in primaries. Yet binding themselves to Trump to avoid primary challenges created insurmountable problems in the general election where “Trump and Trumpism have become toxic,” Ayres said.

That same conundrum looms over the potential 2028 Republican presidential field, particularly Vice President JD Vance. Trump is likely to fire social media thunderbolts against any attempt from Vance or other candidates to meaningfully distance from him, and no one seeking the nomination can afford too much conflict with the president, given his durable popularity with the MAGA base. Yet if Trump remains anywhere near as unpopular with the broad public as he is today, failing to separate from him could prove fatal for the eventual GOP nominee in the general election.

Vance himself seems to be aware of this catch-22; CNN reported last week that the vice president has given serious consideration to not running for president in 2028 in the wake of the GOP’s disastrous midterm performance.

There’s little sign Republicans will change course

All this underscores the GOP’s stake in Trump mounting at least some recovery by 2028. A decisive conclusion to the Iran War that lowered gas and diesel prices might lift him somewhat.

But Democratic pollster Anna Greenberg said it will be extremely difficult for Trump to regain much of the allegiance he lost over the past two years among the new voters who moved toward him in 2024 — particularly Hispanic Americans, Black men and younger men. Most of those voters, she said, feel not only disappointed but angry at Trump for failing to alleviate their economic squeeze as he promised — while focusing so much on his own priorities, like building monuments and padding his fortune.

“Especially for the people who are less ideologically committed to him… the betrayal and the broken promises make it very hard to come back from,” Greenberg said. “It’s not just the bad job performance.”

As problematic, Trump and congressional Republicans show no sign of rethinking the course that ran the party into this electoral ditch. Instead, through the elevation of the belligerent hard-liners Miller and Jordan, the GOP has not only ignored but actively rejected the voters’ roar of discontent.

Add the prospect of extensive congressional hearings exposing corruption and self-dealing in the administration and many analysts believe Trump’s approval rating could fall even lower by 2028. “He may not be at his lowest point,” saud Emory University political scientist Alan Abramowitz, who has extensively studied the relationship between election outcomes and presidential approval. “He is going to have a hard time clawing his way back up to anything higher than he is now, given what is likely to be happening” with investigations and the economy.

If Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio wins the GOP nomination in 2028, they might find it especially difficult to escape negative feelings about Trump, since they served so closely with him. But, as Abramowitz said, “every prominent Republican has tied themselves closely to Trump over the past two years.”

Though voters still harbor many doubts about Democrats, if Trump can’t repair his public standing, those Democratic vulnerabilities may not matter as much as Republicans hope — just as they did little to stop the massive blue tide earlier this month.

news.title: Democrats look to what’s next after Trump. But first, an actual party
news.text:
But the vibes among the hundreds of party operatives, strategists and would-be 2028 presidential candidates who gathered to ask what’s next after nearly a decade of living in President Donald Trump’s shadow?

Party on, Wayne! Party on, Garth!

Democrats arguably haven’t had such a wide-open presidential field since the “Wayne’s World” era, when a preternaturally talented Southern state governor named Bill Clinton came almost out of nowhere to win the White House in 1992.

Now, Democrats have exploded out of a Trump-imposed political wilderness to their most sweeping midterm win since Watergate. And they were ready to take a beat before they begin what’s sure to be a frenzied season of presidential campaign announcements, hiring, fundraising and knife-fighting among a dozen or more White House hopefuls.

Even the would-be candidates could barely hide their elation during donor dinners, at hotel rooftop receptions, and over drinks at the bar at the Ritz-Carlton in downtown Denver, where many mingled late into the night.

But on the main stage, on the first day, those gathered here were warned: Voters still aren’t all that into them.

“These voters that we lost and that we have turned away are still out there and they have not become Democrats yet,” influential Democratic data guru David Shor said as the two-day gathering kicked off. “They will be here in two years, and if we have not persuaded them by then, we might not be happy with how things turn out.”

There was no agreement about how to do that. The prescriptions coming from the stage previewed the struggle that’s beginning to emerge: Did Tuesday’s wins signal an uncompromising fighter from the party’s left wing can dominate the nominating contest and go on to win a national election?

Or is the message that to win everywhere, the party should choose someone who can appeal to the voters who rejected the woke culture-war politics of the Covid era?

“The American people cannot wait two years for change. So we must work with President Trump,” said Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico.

“The only way we’re going to fix that is by fixing it together. We can’t do it with the same warfare that brought us here,” said Rob Sand, the incoming Democratic governor of Iowa.

Contrast those two millennial red-state newcomers with Democratic Rep. Ro Khanna, who hails from deep-blue California, co-chaired Bernie Sanders’ presidential campaign in 2020, and is widely expected to run for president in 2028 as an unapologetic progressive.

“This is not the 1990s. We cannot cobble together a fleeting big tent through perpetual triangulating, straddling, and calculating,” Khanna said onstage. The reference to “triangulating” was an unmistakable jab at a buzzword of the Clinton era.

The gathering offered a few reminders of the anger emanating from the party’s base. Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen spoke after announcing he would challenge Chuck Schumer to be the next Senate majority leader.

Likely incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries was heckled by the audience, with one person yelling Jeffries was “a f**king liar!” before being escorted from the hall.

And protesters gathered outside the security perimeter, holding signs that read, “Abolish billionaires,” “No Schumer coronation,” and “No more do-nothing Democrats.” A Denver SWAT vehicle was parked between them and the rideshare dropoff line.

But inside that perimeter and off the stage, all the divisions evaporated into an atmosphere of celebration bordering on elation. There were food trucks parked outside the brewery serving local craft beers on draft. There were musical acts performing in the outdoor plaza in between speeches. Both days were about 65 degrees and sunny, with the weather clear enough to see the mountains.

And it was very cozy and comfortable after hours at at the Ritz bar. The drinks started flowing Thursday night, with Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, who’s considering a presidential run, holding court. Pete Buttigieg was also spotted there Thursday night, as was Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro.

And Friday evening, the nationwide FAA ground stop stranded everyone in Denver at least for a few hours. Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin sat with Govs. Abigail Spanberger of Virginia and Mikie Sherill of New Jersey until the stop was lifted. Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock huddled off the record with reporters. Buttigieg was back too, spotted snapping a selfie or two. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker couldn’t attend the conference, but his team was at the Ritz bar too. So were operatives with ties to Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly and a handful of others.

This was where the conference’s real business unfolded. A top priority was recruiting staff and making connections for presidential campaigns that are set to start kicking off as soon as January, if not earlier, according to conversations with over a dozen strategists and operatives with ties to presidential hopefuls.

Much of the chatter and speculation focused on possible candidates who weren’t in the room, Kamala Harris and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez chief among them. Their decisions to run or not to run for president in 2028 will fundamentally shape the rest of the field.

Wins across the South underscore the power of Black voters, already perhaps the most important single constituency in any Democratic primary, and Harris starts with an enormous advantage there, especially among Black women.

And then there’s the progressive wing, energized by victories from working-class candidates and people like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan.

“People are thinking there’s more room for someone on the left, and wondering if it means AOC is going to run,” said one top operative with close ties to a likely 2028 Democratic presidential candidate.

There was also widespread speculation about Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, whose been widely considered a top-tier likely 2028 contender. At the heart of his appeal had been the argument he can win big in one of the most important swing states on the map. Now, he’s got a lot of competition from newer faces in the party.

“I’m proud to be the governor of what I think is the swingiest state in America, but we got a lot of company now,” Shapiro told me in an interview. “Look at Texas, look at South Carolina, Iowa, and a whole lot more. But I think that presents an opportunity for Democrats not to be thinking about how to get to 270 on an electoral map, but get to 370 back how Obama won and Clinton won.”

Other potential contenders, including California Gov. Gavin Newsom and Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, also didn’t appear here. Newsom, who had occupied something of frontrunner status in the invisible primary as he jabbed at Trump over the past year, seemed to have faded somewhat from the main conversation, at least in these halls.

(Newsom hasn’t faded, apparently, for Trump, who spent part of his weekend attacking Newsom for commuting the death sentences of all California inmates on death row and changing them to life without parole.)

As the hundreds of Democrats who gathered here struggled to find a way out of Denver, the airport chaos almost presaged what could be a massive post-Trump hangover for a party that’s elated but set for a bruising internal struggle over what’s next.

“If you ask the American people, there is no question about who we oppose,” said Massachusetts Rep. Jake Auchincloss. “But also no sense of what we believe. That is the question we have to answer right now.”

news.text:
They haven’t even been sworn in yet, and Democrats are already starting to make fools of themselves. They’re planning to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth – apparently for the crime of being a MAGAn, because their official reason, “we don’t like the way he’s handling the war” would bring the process to new levels of absurdity. What next, impeach the Treasury secretary because you don’t agree with his tax policies?

Republicans certainly shouldn’t point fingers, though, because they’re the biggest fools of all. Both major parties engaged in a duel of buffoonery this election cycle, as they almost always do. It seemed as if they tried to outdo one another in terms of hypocrisy and incompetence. Congratulations, Republicans, you out-imbeciled your opponents, causing them to win by default.
Let’s begin with Texas. Never mind that Republican incumbent John Cornyn would’ve fared much better against Democrat winner James Talarico than did troubled Ken Paxton, whose scandal-ridden past was a liability from the moment he primaried Cornyn – helped by President Trump’s endorsement, apparently due to Cornyn’s failure to demonstrate absolute loyalty to him, as Trump saw it. Governor Greg Abbott also lost his 12-year stronghold on the Lone Star State to Latina Gina Hinojosa. Certainly sweeping changes in Texas’ demographics caused Democrats to prevail, but those same Latino voters went for Trump two years earlier. What happened? It’s very simple: Republicans embarked on a years-long campaign to convince minority voters that the Democrats – the party they long-trusted – had done nothing for them, and implored them to give the GOP a chance. After all, as Trump himself posited the question: “what have you got to lose?” When Republicans let them down, it was easy to jump ship.

Abbott prided himself on tough policies concerning PHIs (Persons Here Illegally). He famously bused PHIs from Texas to Kamala Harris’ home, and to Martha’s Vineyard, a posh vacation spot for wealthy progressives who tend to show empathy for the have-nots as long as it’s not in their own backyard. However, after Trump squandered immigration enforcement – the one issue that put him over the top in 2016, besting a powerhouse field of 16 other Republicans, including five senators and nine governors – because his ICE flunkies exhibited behavior that Texans like to call: “all hat and no cattle.”

Both parties are notorious for insulting voters’ intelligence, underestimating their ability to discern patently misleading ads; but again, Republicans outdid them in terms of backfired strategies. Take Talarico, who, in his own words, said our borders should be like a front porch with a giant welcome mat. Republicans from Trump on down repeated those words incessantly – conveniently omitting the second part of Talarico’s statement: “with a lock on the front door.” It makes knowledgeable voters angry and resentful to hear their own party prey on other voters’ ignorance. Always quick to give a foe a nickname, Trump dubbed the Democratic hopeful ‘Talafreako’. If it didn’t sound clever enough when he said it, it sounded a thousand times worse when his MAGA sycophants repeated it. I mean, if Elvis is flat on a note, that’s not good, but if Elvis impersonators sing off key, they’re absolute laughing stocks.

Back to the Democrats: sure, they won by default, but let’s not think they’re incapable of being every bit as idiotic as Republicans. Odds are, in two years we’ll be talking about an impending Red Wave, and news anchors will be describing GOP victories as “stunning.”

As I explain to my Republican friends – talking them down from the ledge as conservative commentators they follow slavishly scare them by lamenting how America is “finished” and warning that these newly elected Democrats will “trans your kids!” – very little is likely to change. You see, if Democrats continue to govern as spitefully as Republicans have for the past two years, and as Democrats did in the time before that, then next to nothing will be done. The Senate has the filibuster, a tool that essentially prevents any bill from advancing without at least 60 votes. Republicans had 53 Senate seats. Democrats fared a little better, but are still below 60. For all the talk about ending the filibuster, that requires 67 votes. Does anyone really think the party out of power would vote to allow the party in power to pass any bill it wants to by a simple majority vote? That’s almost as ridiculous as expecting states like Idaho and Wyoming to vote directly against their own interests and do away with the Electoral College.

What if Democrats can manage to pull a small handful of Republicans over to their side and amass the necessary 60 votes? Well, then, the president would have to agree with the legislation, or else he can veto it. And how does Congress overcome a veto? – by a two-thirds majority. Despite all the Blue Wave hoopla, the Democrats are nowhere close to a veto-proof supermajority.
In short, expect another two years of a Do-Nothing Congress, this time with Democrats at the helm. But there’s one way out: think back to Bill Clinton’s presidency.
Clinton, a Democrat, had to work with Republicans in control of Congress during the final six years of his presidency. He compromised. He famously uttered the words “the era of big government is over” in a State of the Union address. That’s how impactful Clinton’s level of concession was. Clinton worked with Republicans: he and House Speaker Newt Gingrich even managed to balance the budget – a feat that’s not been accomplished since.

Will Trump come to the table and work with Democrats? He’s stubborn as a mule, but he does pride himself on making deals.
