news.title: These 8 Democratic women with military experience flipped GOP House seats
news.text:
Centrist Democrats are celebrating a new group of eight female veterans joining the House of Representatives.

"Meet the badass service women heading to Congress," Michigan Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin wrote in a Nov. 9 social media post that included a graphic with the words, "Service women are fighting back."

The new group represents an expansion of a trend that started in the last Democratic midterm election wave. In fact, one of the new members was first elected then.

Rep.-elect Elaine Luria, D-Virginia, was first elected to Congress in 2018, after serving for 20 years in the U.S. Navy before retiring as a commander, along with Naval Academy graduate and helicopter pilot Mikie Sherrill of New Jersey, former CIA officer Abigail Spanberger of Virginia and former U.S. Air Force captain Chrissy Houlahan of Pennsylvania. Slotkin was also sent to Congress from Michigan that year after working as a CIA analyst, touring Iraq and working in White House and Pentagon national security roles. All were Democrats.

Earlier in 2026, Slotkin and Houlahan were among the six Democrats who went viral for a video telling troops not to obey illegal orders. On Truth Social, President Donald Trump called that action “seditious” and said it could be “punishable by DEATH!”

Luria lost her Virginia Beach-area swing district seat in 2022, but now she will return to Congress after taking her seat from Rep. Jen Kiggans, the Republican who had beaten her.

The former and future Virginia congresswoman, Luria, will be joined by a new crop of servicewomen heading to Congress, all of whom flipped Republican seats.

In South Carolina, Nancy Lacore, a former Navy Vice Admiral, was fired by Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth after 35 years of military service, but flipped outgoing Republican Rep. Nancy Mace's Charleston district over a Republican challenger.

Rep.-elect Rebecca Bennett was inspired by Sherrill, a fellow former Navy helicopter pilot, and Spanberger to run against New Jersey Republican Rep. Tom Kean Jr.

National security officer Cait Conley defeated New York Republican Rep. Mike Lawler. JoAnna Mendoza, the first woman Marine elected to Congress, beat Republican Rep. Juan Ciscomani in Arizona, and ex-Air Force officer Kristina Knickerbocker won over Republican Rep. Mike Turner in a reliably red Ohio district.

Army veteran Jessica Killin prevailed over Republican Rep. Jeff Crank in Colorado, while in a neighboring Colorado district, former Navy Rear Adm. Eileen Laubacher ousted MAGA firebrand Rep. Lauren Boebert.

They join other women in Congress with military experience, including Houlahan, Sen. Tammy Duckworth, D-Illinois, Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, R-Florida, and Rep. Maggie Goodlander, D-New Hampshire.

More: Trump ally Lauren Boebert narrowly trails Dem challenger in close race

While Luria was out of Congress, Slotkin was elected to the Senate in 2024, even as Trump carried her state. In 2025, Spanberger was elected governor of Virginia and Sherrill won the governor's race in New Jersey.

"You're like, 'OK, if they can do it, so can I,'" Bennett told USA TODAY about Sherrill and Spanberger's wins in 2018. "They were kind of what gave me the confidence to be able to just try to do this as, you know, kind of a political outsider."

Introducing the 'Hell Cats'

During Trump's first term, Luria, Sherill, Slotkin, Spanberger and Houlahan were cast as a more moderate bunch of incoming congresswomen, contrasted by the media with progressive Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez's "Squad," which also included Reps. Ayanna Pressley, Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib.

While the Squad all represent safe Democratic House districts, the ex-service members have demonstrated an ability to win in swing districts and statewide races.

More: Why are they called the 'Squad'? How four freshman Democrats got their group nickname

This cycle, a new group of women banded together and formed the "Hell Cats." Bennett in New Jersey, Arizona's Mendoza, Conley in New York and Maura Sullivan, a former Marine captain who lost in the New Hampshire primary, were members in a quartet that shared a group chat on the commercial messaging app Signal, according to The 19th News, and discussed strategy.

Sullivan lost her primary to Stefany Shaheen, the daughter of New Hampshire Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, but the rest of the candidates faced Republican incumbents in their general election matchups.

And while the Squad draws headlines for promoting progressive policies like the Green New Deal and feuds with the Democratic establishment, such as Tlaib not endorsing then-Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential race, the ex-service members have cut a more moderate path.

A nonprofit that ranks members for bipartisan efforts put Spanberger at fifth, Slotkin at 12th and Sherrill at 50th, out of the 435 House members, in the 117th Congress from 2021 to 2023.

Hegseth fired Nancy Lacore from Navy. Now he could help her get to Congress

In Sherill's and Spanberger's 2025 gubernatorial campaigns, they emphasized their national security backgrounds and cruised to victory in their Democratic-leaning states.

This cycle, Conley faced off against New York Rep. Lawler, who tried to brand himself as one of the most moderate members of Congress, even after Trump campaigned with him. Conley's messaging on affordability and national security prevailed in a district that had reelected Lawler in 2024, despite simultaneously favoring Harris over Trump.

Lacore in South Carolina flipped her district by 1 percentage point, after Mace – who this cycle ran for South Carolina governor and lost in the primary – turned it red in 2020. In 2024, Mace beat her Democratic opponent by 16 points.

In New Jersey, Bennett succeeded in a swing district that Trump won in 2024 but Sherrill carried for governor in 2025. Bennett avoided her opponent's mental-health-related absence from Capitol Hill in the spring, instead focused on Kean Jr.'s voting record in support of Trump and her own time as a naval helicopter pilot.

Why so many Democratic women with military backgrounds run

VoteVets, an organization that works to give veterans a bigger say and supports Democratic veterans, supported the women veteran candidates in the 2026 cycle.

Kayla Williams, senior adviser to VoteVets and an Army veteran who deployed to Iraq in 2003-2004, said that women veterans are appealing candidates because they come not only with their service experience, but also juggling home and family lives and being grassroots Americans who can relate to everyday challenges.

"Candidates like this come to public office with a unique perspective that no one else has, and it resonates," Williams told USA TODAY in an email.

Williams slammed Hegseth for comments about women in military combat roles, saying, "Despite everything Pete Hegseth wants you to believe, women are on the front lines of defending America every day around the world and, like myself, have been deployed to war."

Still, the new group of Democratic women veterans flipped seats by often-tight margins, which might put their seats in play in a more favorable year for Republicans. Laubacher leads Boebert by less than 1 point in a district that hasn't been represented by a Democrat since 2011.

More hawkish stances on national security can be risky in Democratic primaries. Sullivan, the veteran "Hell Cat" who lost her primary in New Hampshire, was slammed by her opponent for campaign spending on her behalf from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee.

Slotkin has also been criticized by fellow Democrats. In 2025, the Progressive Caucus of the Michigan Democratic Party complained that she "more closely aligns herself with Republicans than her proclaimed constituents" in a social media post.

But some of the servicewomen are eager to confront Republicans over national security. On Nov. 12, Conley posted a clip in which she called Hegseth a "harm" to national security and pledged that, "if the 119th Congress won’t impeach him, the 120th Congress will."

Conley told USA TODAY that, despite their shared military background, when they talked at congressional orientation, "the biggest focus for our group, and really the broader freshman class, is lowering costs and rooting out corruption."

"In the pledge that all of us made to our constituents was to get in here and to get stuff done," Conley told USA TODAY. "That's the background we bring, right? We come from worlds where talk is cheap. Action is everything and we are a results-oriented group of leaders."

news.title: An Unrepentant Biden Defends Reelection Decision In New Book
news.text:
Former US President Joe Biden defends his decision to run for reelection in 2024 with a vigor he could not typically muster during the race itself, in his memoir set for release on Tuesday, and downplays the impact of a disastrous debate performance while insisting his critics could “never point to something presidential I had failed to do.”

HuffPost obtained an advanced copy of the 465-page book, titled Promise Me, America, which Biden will likely be limited in promoting due to his ongoing battle with prostate cancer. The book contains no indications the Delawarean has any regrets from his presidency, whether it be how he addressed foreign crises in Ukraine and Gaza, how he handled recalcitrant senators in pursuing his domestic agenda or in his decision to mount a reelection bid at age 82. 

“People say I was deluding myself that I could do the job at my age,” Biden writes of his decision to run again. “My answer to that is: I was doing the job.”

The final chapters of the book, which cover his decision to run again, his ultimate ouster as the party’s nominee and former Vice President Kamala Harris’ eventual loss after taking over as the Democratic candidate, function as a self-portrait of a man determined to snap back at his critics. 

He lingers on his victories in the essentially uncontested Democratic primaries in 2024, viewing the results as something more than fait accompli acknowledgments of reality. He brushes aside the idea his age was a real handicap in office, instead portraying it as more of an aesthetic barrier — one he was trying to conquer with help from then-Sen. Mitt Romney (R-Utah), who had told him to lengthen his stride in public. He claims perceptions of his debate performance were shaped more by the media and party elites than by his own incoherence onstage. 

 “The press and the pundits had decided my performance was fatal,” he writes, insisting polling data did not show him suffering in the race against Trump — even though internal Democratic polls from the time showed him in danger of losing the blue states of Virginia, New Jersey, New Mexico, Maine and New Hampshire. He adds: “But the data wasn’t the point. The narrative was. And the narrative was bad. There was a consensus that I had lost. Worse than that, there was a consensus that it couldn’t be fixed.” 

Biden, whose self-image has always tended towards jovial grandfather, stays away from the harsh vitriol a different man might uncork in such a book. But his bitterness over what he feels is a lack of press respect for his accomplishments and treacherous behaviour by fellow Democrats like Nancy Pelosi and Chuck Schumer nonetheless comes through. 

Recounting a NATO summit he hosted in the days following the debate, he notes some press coverage focused more on a verbal gaffe — he had called Harris “Vice President Trump” by mistake — than on his accomplishment. 

“It was a perfect example of what was happening to me. The fact that I was leading a stronger and more united NATO than the world had ever seen — and leading the effort to stand against the worst aggression seen in Europe since World War II — didn’t matter. But mixing up Harris and Trump?” he writes. “That was a big deal.”

Biden also repeatedly turns to Trump to justify his own actions, insisting there was no way the American public would ever choose Trumpian chaos over his steady leadership. And the threat of Trump is why he had no choice but to run again: “I was the only person who had ever beaten Donald Trump,” he writes. “And I felt I was the best person to do it again.”

Democrats largely kept their distance from Biden, who ended his time in office as the least popular Democratic president in four decades, as they swept both chambers of Congress during this year’s midterm elections. Many in the party were not-so-secretly happy Biden’s book was not arriving until well after Election Day. 

But while almost everyone in the party now agrees Biden should not have tried to run again, other recollections are likely to restart intra-party disputes. He recounts how he felt, in the days following Hamas’ massacre of Israelis on October 7, 2023, that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s response would be “overwhelming” in order to “compensate for what was close to dereliction of duty on his part.” 

But any regret about how his administration would handle the subsequent attack on Gaza is limited. “Too many innocent Palestinians were killed,” he writes. “Too much pain was inflicted on people with no connection to Hamas. Too little food and water and medicine and fuel got into Gaza for too long. And I carry that with me.”

“It was a tragedy,” he continues. “A tragedy that worsened under a new administration.”

news.title: Gavin Newsom Reveals When He’ll Decide on 2028 Presidential Run
news.text:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) said Thursday he expects to decide in early January whether to run for president in 2028, around the time his second term as governor ends.

“We’ll spend the next few weeks with the family and make a decision early January,” Newsom told Turkey’s state-run Anadolu news agency during a trip to Antalya for the United Nations climate summit.

Newsom had spoken about a possible White House run before, but until Thursday he hadn’t said when he’d make up his mind.

In a September interview with CNN’s Jake Tapper, the governor said he would need the support of his wife and four children to run. Newsom is barred by California’s term limits from seeking a third term as governor. He also told Tapper he would sit out the race if former Vice President Kamala Harris sought the Democrat nomination.

“I don’t know if she runs, but we’ll see,” Newsom said. “But I wouldn’t run if she ran.”

Fewer California voters are excited about a Newsom presidential run. A September poll from UC Berkeley’s Citrin Center and Politico found that 37% of registered voters in the state said they’d be excited about a Newsom bid, down from 48% in March. Harris’s numbers fell from 41% to 28% over the same period.

Newsom gave his January timetable a little more than a week after Democrats won control of the House and Senate. The party took Senate seats in Kansas, Iowa and Texas and picked up more than two dozen House districts, including some Trump had carried by double digits in 2024.

news.title: Democrat Ro Khanna Is Considering A Presidential Bid. He Could Be The Progressive Wing's Candidate.
news.text: California Congressman and Democrat Ro Khanna has said that, following the Democrats' landslide victory in the recent midterm elections, he is considering a presidential run in 2028."I'm certainly considering it, there are going to be bold progressives ... I'm going around the country, seeing whether the message will resonate ... According to a New York Times average of the last 15 polls on the Democrats' 2028 nominee, former presidential candidate Kamala Harris, California Governor Gavin Newsom, New York Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff, as well as Mark Kelly and Pete Buttigieg, are leading the Democratic pack.Ocasio-Cortez, like Khanna, firmly belongs to the Democrats' progressive wing, and could command significant left-wing support.Nevertheless, Khanna's name recognition has been boosted significantly since the re-election of President Donald Trump to office.Khanna, alongside Republican Congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky, was one of the leading sponsors of the Epstein Files Transparency Act, a bill that made files relating to the criminal activities of the late financier and convicted child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein publicly available.The move made Khanna popular amongst progressives and wider sections of the American electorate.His wider economic vision also makes him a likely contender for the progressive camp heading into 2028; his self-described platform of "economic patriotism" proposes introducing a wealth tax on billionaires, guaranteeing "healthcare as a fundamental right, free and universal for every American," expanding child care access and funding of public schools and colleges as well as ending U.S. financial aid to Israel.In the immediate aftermath of the midterms, allies of Khanna's launched a committee, named "Run Ro," dedicated to laying the groundwork for the representative's presidential campaign if he decides to run.

news.title: MAGA Is Scaring Away Republicans’ Most Loyal Voting Bloc
news.text:
Millions of evangelical Christian voters are abandoning Donald Trump in a massive warning that one of his most important power bases is eroding, a bombshell new analysis has found. 

The Washington Post has revealed that midterm election data from 343 counties with large concentrations of white evangelical voters show that voter turnout was just 66 percent of what it was in 2024. 

Data from the ACP Social Science Lab at Michigan State University shows that while Trump won in those areas by a margin of 62 points, Republican Senate candidates enjoyed just a 45-point advantage in this month’s election. 

Turnout in the heavily white evangelical counties was far lower than in nearby counties, where it was around 78 percent of its 2024 level, according to the Post. The low turnout likely played a key role in the GOP’s sweeping midterm losses, as Democrats seized control of the House and Senate and made inroads in traditionally deep-red states, including Kansas, South Carolina, Iowa, and others.

In typically ruby-red Mississippi, voters elected Democrat Scott Colom as the state’s first Black senator since the 19th century, signaling a shifting balance of power. 

“Those changes may have led to the Republican loss of the Mississippi U.S. Senate seat, surprising big Democratic margins in a few Senate races, and several Democratic pickups of GOP-held U.S. House seats around the country,” Dante Chinni, founder of ACP, told the Post.

White evangelicals have long been among the core elements of Trump’s MAGA movement, according to PRRI data. They backed Trump by 81 percent to 17 percent for Kamala Harris in 2024. 

But Trump’s policies are corroding his evangelical support, with voters concerned about the rising cost of living, the war with Iran, and allegations that Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself. A Pew Research survey ahead of the midterms found that while 78 percent of white evangelicals approved of the president at the start of his second term. That number has since dropped to 58 percent—a flashing red light for the Republican Party. 

In April, Trump deleted an AI-generated image depicting himself as a Jesus-like figure after it provoked a furious backlash from white evangelicals and other Christian communities. 

Trump’s support from white evangelicals had been bolstered in 2022 when Trump appointed justices to the Supreme Court who voted to overturn Roe v. Wade, long a key aim of the pro-life right.

news.title: Westerners Don’t Want Their Utilities Tied To California’s Power Market, Poll Shows
news.text:
A federal power agency is weighing whether to join a California-operated electricity market, but most Westerners polled say their utilities should stay independent.

A draft decision on which day-ahead electricity market the Bonneville Power Administration will join is expected in December, Bonneville senior spokesperson Kevin Wingert said in a statement to the Daily Caller News Foundation. The agency had proposed in March to join a rival to the California market, Markets+.

Seventy-two percent of adults surveyed in five Western media markets said their local utility should stay “independently governed.” Just 10 percent would rather see it coordinate with a “California-run system,” the council’s slides show. The remaining 19 percent said they were not sure.

Causeway Solutions ran the poll for the Western Energy Markets Integrity Council. The advocacy group opposes putting Bonneville’s federal hydropower in what it called a “California-centric trading platform.”

“Pushing these federal assets into the hands of California will have profound adverse consequences for affordability and reliability of power in a region that can ill afford it,” the council said in an Oct. 22 statement to the DCNF.

“The council is an independent not-for-profit organization that receives contributions from power providers and consumers, and individuals. It coordinates with other public interest groups,” Scott Segal, a Bracewell LLP partner speaking for the council, said in a statement. His statement did not name any of those contributors.

“It’s good for California. It’s just bad for everybody else that joins with them,” H. Sterling Burnett, director of the Arthur B. Robinson Center on Climate and Environmental Policy at the Heartland Institute, told the DCNF in a Tuesday interview.

When the DCNF asked who would get power if the whole West ran short, Burnett said, “Well, the big dog eats first.”

He compared it to fights over the Colorado River, saying California gets the most water when there are shortages.

“They have the representatives in the House. They have the biggest population. They get it first,” Burnett said of California.

“California’s disastrous energy policies should serve as a warning to every Western state and no state should allow Sacramento to export its failures across state lines,” Oliver McPherson-Smith, vice chair for energy and environment policy at the America First Policy Institute, said in a statement to the DCNF.

“Customers in other Western states have good reason to resist putting their electricity bills and reliability under the influence of California politicians they didn’t elect and cannot hold accountable,” Jason Isaac, founder and CEO of the American Energy Institute, said in a statement. “Accountability should stay with the people who pay the bills.”

“The Department of Energy is committed to ensuring that American families and businesses, including those across the Pacific Northwest, have access to affordable, reliable, and secure electricity,” a department spokesperson said in a statement to the DCNF.

“Markets+ provides independent governance today,” the Southwest Power Pool, which would run Markets+, said in a statement. “More than one market in the West promotes choice and competition, which enables better outcomes for all participants and states.”

The California Independent System Operator did not respond to the DCNF’s request for comment. (RELATED: Data Center Boom Sparks Battle Over Power Costs, New Regulations)

Independence came out ahead in each market. Support ran from 64 percent in the Billings, Montana, area to 81 percent in the Tri-Cities of Washington.

Those two results carry margins of error of 4.7 points in Billings and 4.9 points in the Tri-Cities, per the slides.

Among the 1,733 people who picked a side, 88 percent chose independence and 12 percent favored coordinating with California.

Eighty-four percent of those surveyed were at least somewhat worried about their electric bills.

Causeway surveyed 2,095 adults, not registered voters, from Sept. 21 to 25 in the Boise, Idaho; Tri-Cities, Washington; Medford, Oregon; Gilbert and Mesa, Arizona; and Billings, Montana, media markets, the council’s polling page says. The text-to-web survey has an overall margin of error of 2.1 percentage points.

Bonneville’s March proposal set a target start date of Oct. 1, 2028, for Markets+. That came after a May 2025 Bonneville policy that put the agency on a path toward Markets+.

That plan is now under review. Bonneville Administrator and CEO Travis Kavulla wrote in a Sept. 3 letter that he had committed to reviewing that course “with fresh eyes.”

He would propose a change in Bonneville’s next draft decision if the agency sees “concrete actions” on governance of the California operator’s market, he wrote. Independent board leadership topped his list.

California revised its laws in 2025 so a separate regional body could govern that market with a board “appointed through an independent process rather than by state actors,” Kavulla noted.

That body, the Regional Organization for Western Energy, is set to interview candidates for its first CEO in December, RTO Insider reported Nov. 11.

“A more unified grid in the West with greater scale, market depth, and more contiguous corridors may alleviate operational and economic risks that would persist in a more fragmented market footprint,” Wingert, Bonneville’s senior spokesperson said. (RELATED: ‘Whole ’Nother Rent’: Soaring Electricity Prices In Kamala Harris’ Home State Are Crushing Residents)

Size is the draw. Leaving out Bonneville’s balancing area, the California operator’s market averaged 39 gigawatts of net generation, against 19 for Markets+. Kavulla cited federal Energy Information Administration data.

The Southwest Power Pool’s website lists an address in Little Rock, Arkansas.

Lawmakers from the Southwest Power Pool’s home state want Bonneville to stay the course. Republican Arkansas Sens. Tom Cotton and John Boozman wrote to Kavulla on Sept. 25 backing Bonneville’s “timely participation” in Markets+.

“The importance of independent governance cannot be overstated,” they wrote. The senators added that the California operator “is and remains statutorily beholden to the interests of the State of California.”

Western Montana’s electric co-op managers said in an Oct. 1 letter to Kavulla that their co-ops “strongly favor SPP.”

Advanced Energy United, which represents clean energy businesses, backed Bonneville’s review in September. The group’s senior director, Brian Turner, said the agency “recognizes the important strides that have been made around governance,” Utility Dive reported.

Bonneville has a workshop on its choice scheduled for Nov. 19, Wingert said.

Kavulla asked the regional body to adopt a framework that lets market participants “initiate and evaluate major market proposals,” with the end of November as his target.

news.title: I Can't Believe Mark Cuban Had the Stones to Say THIS About the Midterms
news.text:
When billionaire investor Mark Cuban went on CNN's The Situation Room on Friday to explain what voters were thinking in the midterms, he delivered one of the most ridiculous takes of the election cycle.

Anchor Pamela Brown set up the question by appealing to his business background. "You're a businessman by nature. If you got these results, what would you do if you were running the country right now?" she asked.

"Fortunately, I'm not. I'm just a business guy. For business people out there, you just keep on doing what you've been doing," Cuban said.

Then he offered his theory of the results. "I mean, in talking to my friends and family, I think people wanted a return to normalcy, you know, more of kind of the standards that we had 10, 15, 20 or more years ago, where people discussed politics, but they weren't rabid about it," he continued.

Sorry, but Mark Cuban's read on the midterms is so very wrong.

I think Cuban torched his reputation when he backed Kamala Harris and her socialist policies in 2024, and he has failed to redeem himself wince then. This comment only digs the hole deeper.

If Cuban wants to talk about who gets rabid over politics, he should look at his own side of the aisle. Democrats are the furthest thing from normal, and they are the ones who treat every political disagreement like a moral emergency. They literally cut off friends and family over who those people voted for. That's the party Cuban spent 2024 cheering on.

On top of that, consider the agenda Democrats have rallied behind. None of it looks like the America of 20 years ago.

Start with gender ideology. Democrats are the party of letting biological males compete in women's sports and of letting biological males who identify as women into women's locker rooms, bathrooms, and other sex-separated spaces. They oppose state and federal limits on puberty blockers, cross-sex hormones, and transition procedures for minors, even as public support for those treatments has slipped.

ICYMI: I Totally Voted for This: Trump Moves to Make Federal Agencies English-Only 

Democrats are also the party of letting children socially transition at school, with new names and pronouns, sometimes without telling their parents. They defend pornographic material in school libraries in the name of LGBTQ inclusivity. And they treat traditional beliefs about biological sex as potential discrimination in schools, workplaces, and public institutions.

I think I’ve already made the case that Cuban is wrong, but I’ll keep going anyway.

When it comes to crime, most normal people want less of it and want to keep themselves and their families safe. But Democrats are the party that embraced "defund the police," entertained abolishing police and prisons outright, and branded law enforcement an inherently racist institution. Democrats have pushed to eliminate cash bail, including for defendants accused of serious crimes, and to scrap mandatory minimum sentences.

And on race, Democrats are the party of reparations funded by today's taxpayers, of racial equity as a factor in virtually every government policy, and of DEI programs that put identity ahead of merit in hiring, education, and government. They view nearly every American institution through the lens of systemic racism and oppression.

Does any of that sound like a return to the standards of 10, 15, or 20 years ago? Voters who want normalcy are running away from this agenda, and Cuban either can't see it or won't admit it.

news.title: Democrats' midterm gains pose fresh challenges for Trump and Republicans: Report
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Nov 14 (IANS) With Democrats holding majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, growing discontent with President Donald Trump is likely to make negotiations with the executive difficult, raising the prospect of prolonged policy paralysis in the United States, a report has said. The Democrat-controlled legislature is also expected to intensify scrutiny of Trump's decisions and his family's financial dealings. Meanwhile, the possibility of impeachment is once again gaining traction in the media, Sanjay Pulipaka, Chairperson of think tank 'Politeia Research Foundation', wrote in India Narrative. “In the Senate, the Democratic Party controls about 54 seats, while the Republican Party holds 44. In the House of Representatives, the Democrats won about 254 seats, while the Republicans won about 162. The Democrats won not only in swing states such as Georgia, Michigan, New Hampshire, and North Carolina, but also in Republican strongholds such as Iowa, Kansas, Texas, and even South Carolina. The scale of anti-incumbency is evident in the fact that, after a few decades, Texas has elected a Democratic senator and a Democratic governor, and Kansas has elected its first Democratic senator since 1932,” Pulipaka noted. “What explains the electoral outcome? It appears that the Iran war has proved to be very costly for the Republican Party. During the 2024 presidential campaign, Donald Trump promised ‘no more wars.’ However, while the intervention in Venezuela turned out to be brief, the Iran War proved to be a different ball game altogether. In fact, Vice President J D Vance noted that the Iran War led to the midterm electoral defeat," he added. According to the report, the Republican Party will reassess its approach after aligning with Trump's agenda before the midterm elections in view of his popularity and electoral success. With Trump's governing style and political approach increasingly proving costly, it said, the Republican Party may reconsider its association with his agenda. Republican leaders with presidential ambitions are reportedly weighing the option of distancing themselves from the Trump administration. The report noted that for the Democratic Party, the challenge now lies in consolidating its gains among voters who have traditionally aligned with the Republicans but recently voted for the Democrats. Its ability to retain these voters remains uncertain, particularly if it reverts to a hardline position on cultural issues, potentially driving them back to the Republican fold. The party's agenda will depend on a new generation of prominent leaders and possible presidential candidates, including Andy Beshear, Gavin Newsom, James Talarico, JB Pritzker, Jon Ossoff, Josh Shapiro, Pete Buttigieg and others, the report mentioned. “Established leaders such as Barack Obama, Rahm Emanuel, Kamala Harris and others should nudge the young leaders to adopt a more prudent strategy. They will have to take note of the fact that many Democrats, such as Senator-elect Talarico (Texas), Senator-elect Adam Hamilton (Kansas) and others, have campaigned ‘around Christian faith and court a segment of voters who had drifted towards Republican’,” India Narrative stated. “The Republicans may have lost this election, but for Democrats to win the Presidential election in 2028, agenda-setting will play a critical role,” it added.

news.title: Biden left Ireland feeling he could ‘be elected president’ here after 2023 visit
news.text:
Former US president Joe Biden has said he left Ireland feeling he could be “elected president” here after his State visit in 2023. 

In extracts from his upcoming memoir Promise Me, America, to be published on November 17th, Biden said the visit “restored my soul and revived my spirit”.

He wrote: “The trip had restored my soul and revived my spirit, which I’d needed. I knew I was headed home for the fight of my political life. 

“I left feeling I could be elected president in Ireland. Now I was about to find out if I could be reelected president in the United States.”

Biden dropped out of the race for the White House the following year after a disastrous debate performance against Donald Trump. He then backed his vice president, Kamala Harris, who secured the Democratic nomination before losing to Trump in 2024. 

Biden also recalled a chance meeting with Fr Frank O’Grady at Knock Shrine. Fr O’Grady, then the US army chaplain at Walter Reed Medical Centre, performed the last rites sacrament on his son Beau Biden, who died of brain cancer in 2015.

“The sight of him brought tears to my eyes,” Biden wrote. 

Biden also said he has good memories of his address at St Muredach’s Cathedral in Ballina on April 14th, 2023, in front of 27,000 “wildly enthusiastic” people. 

“The trip was an emotionally resonant one for me.”

[ Hunter Biden: My father beat Trump ‘like a drum’Opens in new window ]

Looking back on the G7 summit in Cornwall, England, in 2021, Biden discussed his anger with Brexit. 

“Brexit threatened to undermine the Good Friday Agreement of 1998, which had done so much good in bringing peace to Northern Ireland. That was important to me, as a proud Irish American. 

“I also disapproved of Brexit for its ultranationalist claims, and for making many promises that could not possibly be kept.”

He believed “populist leaders and opportunists” had “sold the British people out” by backing Brexit. 

However, he said he “preferred to work out our differences in private”, particularly because former UK prime minister Boris Johnson was the host of the event. 

In another notable section, Biden reveals his admiration for the late Queen Elizabeth, despite being on record about his Irish American mother’s anti-English sentiment. 

[ Civil liberties group criticises Garda response to Joe Biden protest at TrinityOpens in new window ]

He also said the queen reminded him of his mother. 

“She and I had a natural rapport, which might have surprised my mother, to put it mildly. Mom’s Irish blood made it difficult for her to admire the British crown, and she remembered historical grievances as if she had experienced them personally. 

“In fact (I can’t believe I’m about to say this), the queen’s steely strength, combined with the glint of humour in her eye, reminded me of no one as much as Catherine Eugenia Finnegan.” 

Biden has often spoken about his admiration for Irish literature and poetry, including the works of Seamus Heaney. 

He reveals he took inspiration from James Joyce in his 2020 inaugural address. 

“In my first letter, I had shared some words attributed to James Joyce: ‘When I die, Dublin will be written on my heart.’ I returned to them here. Because of you, Delaware will forever be written on my heart. I’ll see you back home.”
news.summary: Former US president remembers his trip to Ireland in several passages in his upcoming memoir Promise Me, America

news.title: The 2028 presidential race is already full of surprises, prediction markets say
news.text: The 2028 presidential election seems far away. Or is it already here? The midterm ballots are barely counted, and a long list of would-be candidates is already elbowing for a lane in a campaign that, by Election Day, will feel like it started during the Truman administration. Outside the Super Bowl, few things are as popular on prediction markets as a presidential race. Two years before anyone casts a ballot, Kalshi's 2028 markets have already drawn nearly half a billion dollars in trading. While prediction markets have an excellent long-term record of accuracy, this far from an election, you can't expect surgical precision. STU BURGUIERE: PUT YOUR MONEY WHERE YOUR MOUTH IS: PREDICTION MARKETS WON THE MIDTERMS What the markets can show us is who's trading like a blue chip, who's stuck in the middle, and whose campaign feels like a penny stock that needs a miracle rally to be competitive. So let's look ahead with a way-too-early presidential market report, starting at the top. The blue chips What if I told you the Democratic front-runner for 2028 is a man a third of Democrats have never heard of? That's what a new Reuters/Ipsos poll found when it comes to Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, and plenty of other Americans are drawing a blank too. Still, a Democrat who wins Georgia by 18 points, in a state President Trump carried in 2024, doesn’t stay anonymous for long. Kalshi gives him a 26% chance of winning the Democratic nomination, the best in the field. Not bad for a guy much of his own party couldn't pick out of a lineup. NEW POLL COMPLICATES VANCE’S STATUS AS TRUMP’S LIKELY 2028 HEIR APPARENT On the Republican side, Vice President J.D. Vance leads the pack, with a 33% chance of winning the nomination but only a 12% chance of winning the presidency. That gap fits what election analyst Nate Silver calls the VP curse. Vice presidents whose bosses are underwater in the polls tend to win their party’s nomination, then lose in November. Then again, Vance has been underestimated before, and he seems to be at his best in high-leverage situations. Both men have also hinted they might not run at all. Coming from politicians, that promise has roughly the credibility of a vow of celibacy from Jensen Huang. The mid-caps California Gov. Gavin Newsom looked like a blue chip a year ago. His chance of winning the Democratic nomination has since cratered from 37% to about 12%. He leaves office in January, which frees him up for a full-time campaign and gives even more airtime to a man who has never been accused of camera shyness. Whether voters want that is another question. AOC TAPS POWER PLAYER WHO HELPED BERNIE SANDERS DEFY THE ODDS AS MAJOR 2028 DECISION LOOMS Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez sits around 13% to win the Democratic nomination. The bigger question is which race she's running in. Traders actually think she's more likely to run for the Senate than for president. Either way, somebody is going to claim the democratic socialist lane. If it's not her, maybe Bernie Sanders takes a third crack at it. He'll only be 87. Like Ocasio-Cortez, Secretary of State Marco Rubio faces a which-job question. He's at 18% to win the Republican nomination, and the market sees him as just as likely to be the running mate as the nominee. VANCE, CRUZ AND DESANTIS DIAGNOSE GOP'S MIDTERM DISASTER AS BATTLE OVER PARTY'S FUTURE BEGINS Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, who ran in 2024 and also leaves office in January, has been the biggest riser in the Republican market since the midterms. He was under 5% to win the nomination before the votes were counted and is now at 17%, nipping at Rubio's heels. The penny stocks Then come the penny stocks. On the Democratic side, that's a crowd in the single digits for the nomination: Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro. Former Vice President Kamala Harris lands here too, a somewhat embarrassing showing for the woman at the top of the ticket two years ago. If you're shopping the bargain bin, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore at 2.2% and Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer at 0.7% might be in your wheelhouse. (In dead last, at 0.0%: Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz.) CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION On the Republican side, the penny stocks include Texas Sen. Ted Cruz and former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin. Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp and Missouri Sen. Josh Hawley could be value plays. And somewhere in that mix is President Donald Trump, who I wouldn't put past publicly flirting with a constitutionally prohibited third run just to annoy the media. The long-term outlook Many of these names won’t make it to the first primary. Today’s penny stock could be next summer’s blue chip. That’s the fun of watching these markets this early: prices will move with every speech, stumble and suspiciously timed book tour between now and then. news.title: Democrats may have found a way around the Electoral College
news.text:
The 2026 midterms were a drubbing for Republicans at nearly every level of government. But there’s an overlooked upshot of the Democrats’ sweep that could effectively alter the U.S. Constitution and the way the country elects its president.

The National Popular Vote Compact is now easily achievable.

I cannot overstate the seismic shift that the NPVC will bring to presidential elections

The NPVC is an agreement among states to assign their Electoral College votes to whoever wins the most votes nationwide in a presidential election, regardless of which candidate wins the most votes in the state. It goes into effect only if enough states join, through state legislation, to ensure the compact states will anoint the winner. Hence the states in the compact must have collectively 270 or more Electoral College votes.

The compact is also a partisan issue — Democrats support it; Republicans oppose it. Until the morning of November 4, the NPVC was stuck at 222 Electoral College votes.

However, with Democrats gaining lawmaking authority — i.e., control of both houses of the state legislature and governorship — in Arizona, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, and Nevada, the NPVC has a clear shot of controlling the outcome of the 2028 election.

If the five newly Democrat-controlled states pass compact legislation, the NPVC will reach 283 Electoral College votes. Any one of Arizona, Wisconsin, or Nevada could not pass NPVC legislation, and the compact will still go into effect.

I cannot overstate the seismic shift that the NPVC will bring to presidential elections, nor ignore the significant constitutional questions it raises.

The NPVC will make every vote cast in every hamlet, town, and metropolis have equal influence in the final tally for president. Traditional swing-state-based electoral strategy will be useless — the goal for presidential campaigns will be to turn out every voter that they can everywhere in the country.

From a democracy perspective, it sounds great. “Every vote equal” is the rallying cry for the NPVC movement. It is not an unalloyed good, though. For folks skeptical of money in politics, the NPVC makes campaigning drastically more expensive.

Take, for example, the closest thing we’ve had to two parties competing on a national scale for every possible vote: the 2026 midterms. Democrats and Republicans actually tried to win every Senate contest, and the result was the most expensive election in American history: close to $12 billion spent.

The high for presidential elections, in 2020, is just over $6 billion, because whole swaths of the country — the South, the Northeast, the Pacific Coast — are uncontested. And the newly opened battlegrounds will be in some of the most expensive places to campaign: New York City, Los Angeles, Chicago, Dallas, and so on.

RELATED: The GOP’s old dogs had better learn some new tricks

 Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

Presidential elections under the NPVC will look a lot more like midterms, and given the higher stakes, the country could easily see more than $20 billion spent for a single office. Presidential election spending will finally catch up with potato chip spending (about $25 billion per year).

In addition to spending, the NPVC raises some thorny legal questions.

Right now, the national popular vote is a fiction calculated by summing 51 separate jurisdictions’ final vote tallies. But each state gets to its final tally in a different way. Some are all mail ballots, others have longer or shorter early voting, and so on. So a vote in Oregon doesn’t really mean the same thing as a vote in Florida.

That’s a significant, nationwide equality problem for the NPVC.

Additionally, since states shifted to awarding their Electoral College votes to the statewide winner in the 1830s, Americans expect their vote to translate to their state’s influence on the outcome. Under the NPVC, each state’s voters lose their unique impact on who becomes president.

For example, think of yourself as an Indian-American voter in California who had the opportunity to express, through California’s electoral votes, your preference for the first candidate of Indian descent, Kamala Harris. With the NPVC, you can’t do that any more, because California’s Electoral College votes would have gone to Donald Trump in 2024.

So the five states that have shifted to unified Democrat control should carefully consider whether they want to join the NPVC. While attractive from an abstract perspective, the compact has significant flaws and downsides.

If the states do join, though, 2028 will be an objectively historic election.
